28	## Core Problem
29	
30	Test-time compute scaling (TTS) dramatically improves LLM reasoning on scalar-answer tasks, but structured prediction outputs — entity sets, relation graphs, event frames, SQL parse trees, dialogue states — have no clear verification function. Adaptive TTS methods (DSC, Slim-SC, ReASC, CGES, Sonata) further optimize compute allocation — but exclusively for scalar answers where consistency is trivially measured by answer agreement. We ask: when and why does sampling multiple schema-constrained structured outputs and aggregating via structural consistency improve prediction quality, how should compute be adaptively allocated across instances of varying structural complexity, and when does TTS fundamentally fail for structured prediction? We demonstrate through information extraction as the primary testbed, while establishing a general-purpose framework applicable to any structured prediction task.
31	
32	## Opportunity / Why Now
33	
34	TTS is the dominant paradigm for boosting LLM reasoning (DeepSeek-R1, o1), and a rapidly growing literature on adaptive TTS — DSC (NAACL 2025 Findings), Slim-SC (EMNLP 2025), ReASC (ACL 2026), CGES (arXiv 2511.02603), Sonata (ICLR 2026), CoRefine (arXiv 2602.08948), 'Learning When to Sample' (arXiv 2603.08999) — demonstrates that confidence-gated early stopping and difficulty-adaptive allocation can reduce sampling budgets by 45-80% with negligible accuracy loss. Yet this entire literature operates on scalar answers where consistency reduces to answer agreement. Two critical findings frame the gap for structured prediction: (1) PMC12888769 shows weak consistency-accuracy correlation for IE using surface-level Fleiss' Kappa on zero-shot models (Spearman 0.20-0.28), but the authors note that fine-tuned models 'could exhibit different consistency-accuracy dynamics'; (2) arXiv 2509.06861 argues TTS cannot help knowledge-intensive tasks because sampling cannot inject new information. We hypothesize that both findings admit an important exception: for fine-tuned models on structured prediction tasks, a significant fraction of errors are uncertainty-based (boundary detection, type ambiguity, structural composition) rather than knowledge-gap errors — and structural consistency (not surface string matching) can identify correct outputs in this regime. Moreover, structural consistency scores provide a natural gating signal for adaptive compute allocation: high early agreement signals easy instances where further sampling is wasteful, while low agreement signals hard instances requiring the full sampling budget. This opportunity extends beyond IE: any LLM task producing structured outputs — SQL queries, code ASTs, clinical FHIR resources, dialogue states — faces the same gap between scalar-answer TTS methods and structured prediction reality. XGrammar (MLSys 2025) makes constrained sampling near-free (<40 microseconds/token via vLLM's default backend), and mature UIE models (ProUIE, GoLLIE) provide strong base samplers. Concurrent work on multi-model NER ensembles (EL4NER, ACL 2025 submission) aggregates across different models, and CSC-SQL applies self-consistency to text-to-SQL via merge revision — but no work provides a general framework for adaptive structural self-consistency from a single fine-tuned model, isolating TTS contribution from model diversity and directly testing whether self-consistency scaling works for structured prediction.
35	
36	## Landscape (SOTA & Limitations)
37	
38	Test-time scaling is extensively studied for math/code (Forest-of-Thought, ICML 2025; Parallel TTS, Oct 2025; 30B+ token study, Dec 2024) but targets scalar-answer tasks exclusively. Self-consistency voting (Wang et al., ICLR 2023) and its successors — Reasoning-Aware Self-Consistency (NAACL 2025), inverse-entropy weighted voting (arXiv Nov 2025), Radial Consensus Score (arXiv April 2026), confidence-informed SC (arXiv Feb 2025), Ranked Voting SC (ACL 2025 Findings) — all aggregate scalar, embedding-space, or ranked-list answers. Critically, a mature and rapidly growing adaptive TTS literature optimizes compute allocation along a clear lineage: DSC (NAACL 2025 Findings) uses difficulty-based batch-level sample pre-allocation, ranking problems by difficulty and partitioning into easy/hard groups to adaptively allocate inference budgets; Slim-SC (EMNLP 2025) dynamically prunes redundant reasoning chains step-by-step during generation based on inter-chain semantic similarity, achieving up to 45% latency reduction; ReASC (ACL 2026) reframes adaptive sampling from response counting to evidence sufficiency via two-stage reliability-aware accumulation achieving 70% cost reduction; CGES (arXiv 2511.02603) forms Bayesian posteriors over candidate answers for principled early stopping with 69.4% call reduction; Sonata (ICLR 2026) trains a lightweight adapter to predict self-consistency from hidden states for thinking budget allocation (20-60% reduction); CoRefine (arXiv 2602.08948) uses a 211k-parameter Conv1D controller for HALT/RETHINK/ALTERNATIVE decisions with 63% wall-clock speedup; 'Learning When to Sample' (arXiv 2603.08999) achieves 80% token reduction via confidence-aware gating. The 'Reasoning on a Budget' survey (arXiv 2507.02076) provides a comprehensive taxonomy of adaptive TTC methods. However, all these methods define consistency and confidence over scalar answers — none addresses structured outputs where consistency measurement itself is non-trivial. In adjacent structured prediction domains, Functional Majority Voting (arXiv 2604.15618) aggregates code generation samples via execution-based functional equivalence — but this relies on executability, inapplicable to IE or most structured prediction tasks. CSC-SQL applies self-consistency with merge revision to text-to-SQL, but uses a task-specific correction model rather than a general structural consistency framework. STED (arXiv 2512.23712, NeurIPS 2025 Workshop) introduces Semantic Tree Edit Distance for measuring consistency of structured JSON outputs using Hungarian algorithm-based order-invariant matching and multi-level similarity, but functions as an evaluation framework rather than an improvement method — it measures consistency without leveraging it for aggregation or adaptive compute allocation. No work defines a general structural self-consistency framework for structured prediction outputs or uses it for adaptive compute gating. In IE specifically, ProUIE (April 2026) achieves SOTA via GRPO with stepwise fine-grained rewards on Qwen3-4B (ACE05-NER: 86.15 F1, ACE05-Arg: 52.58 F1, SciERC: 46.76 F1, avg NER: 79.44, avg RE: 71.17), and MR-UIE (Sept 2025) applies multi-perspective reasoning with RL — but both are training-time methods that generate single-pass outputs at inference. Post-hoc correction approaches include VerifiNER (ACL 2024) using KB-grounded verification and EL4NER (arXiv 2505.23038) ensembling multiple small LLMs for NER — but these are KB-dependent or multi-model approaches, fundamentally different from single-model self-consistency with adaptive gating. SaM (ACL 2025) dynamically selects and merges domain-specific NER expert models, again a multi-model approach. PMC12888769 (2026) measured consistency-accuracy correlation using Fleiss' Kappa on zero-shot hard-prompted models, finding weak Spearman correlations (0.20-0.28) — but used surface string matching on un-fine-tuned models while we propose structural consistency on task-specific fine-tuned models, and they acknowledged this limitation. The 'Two Failures of Self-Consistency' (Chen et al., 2023) demonstrates poor compositional consistency — IE has compositional structure (entity to relation to event) that may exhibit similar failures, which we explicitly test. No concurrent work applies adaptive test-time sampling with structural aggregation from a single fine-tuned model to any structured prediction task — confirmed via arXiv and OpenReview searches through May 2026.
39	
40	## Proposed Approach
41	
42	We propose Adaptive Structural Self-Consistency Scaling (AS2CS) as both a method and an empirical framework for understanding when adaptive TTS helps structured prediction, demonstrated through information extraction as a comprehensive testbed. The research is structured in three phases: pilot validation (Phase 0), full experimental study (Phase 1), and adaptive gating evaluation (Phase 2).
43	
44	**Phase 0: Pilot Validation and Headroom Analysis (~8h H100, Days 1-3)**
45	Before committing to the full study, we run a targeted pilot to validate two premises. First, using 200 instances each from ACE05 NER and ACE05 EAE (event argument extraction), we sample N=8 extractions at T=1.0 from fine-tuned Qwen3-8B and compute: (a) Fleiss' Kappa on surface string matches (replicating PMC12888769), (b) our soft Jaccard span-level structural consistency score, and (c) Spearman correlation of each metric with per-instance F1 against gold annotations. If structural consistency yields significantly stronger correlation than Fleiss' Kappa (target: Spearman >=0.40 vs. their 0.20-0.28), we proceed. Second, we compute oracle best-of-N F1 gaps per dataset and subtask at N=8 to establish headroom ceilings: if oracle best-of-8 exceeds single-pass by <1 F1 on a subtask, TTS gains are fundamentally ceiling-limited there. We use headroom gaps to prioritize analysis: high-headroom subtasks (likely EAE at ~52 F1, SciERC RE at ~47 F1) receive full experimental treatment, while low-headroom subtasks (likely ACE05 NER near ~87 F1) are analyzed primarily for negative/diagnostic insight. Phase 0 also generates training data for the learned aggregation scorer (Phase 2). If both metrics show weak correlation (<=0.30) even with structural consistency, we pivot to a negative/analytical result.
46	
47	**Base Models**: Qwen3-8B fine-tuned on UIE instruction data (JSON output format, trained with LLaMA Factory following ProUIE's pipeline) as primary model, and GoLLIE-7B as a cross-architecture generalization check.
48	
49	**Sampling**: For each input, we sample N in {4, 8, 16, 32} schema-constrained extractions via XGrammar-backed structured generation in vLLM with temperature T=1.0 (standard for self-consistency sampling, maximizing output diversity), enforcing valid JSON output at near-zero overhead.
50	
51	**Phase 1: Structural Consistency Aggregation (Full Study)**
52	Three aggregation functions tailored to IE subtask structure: (1) span-level entity voting via soft Jaccard similarity over character offsets with type-aware grouping (threshold tau_span), (2) relation-level graph consensus via edge majority voting after entity coreference alignment using mention overlap (threshold tau_coref), (3) event-level frame aggregation via trigger-anchored slot matching with role-wise majority voting (threshold tau_trigger). A composite structural agreement score ranks candidates or constructs a merged consensus output.
53	
54	**Aggregation Hyperparameter Sensitivity Analysis**: Each aggregation function depends on a threshold parameter. We report sensitivity sweeps: tau_span in {0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.8}, tau_coref in {0.3, 0.5, 0.7}, tau_trigger in {0.5, 0.7, 0.9}. We report F1 variance across threshold settings per dataset.
55	
56	**Phase 2: Adaptive Gating and Learned Aggregation**
57	
58	*Adaptive Structural Consistency Gating (ASCG)*: Rather than applying a fixed N=32 samples uniformly, we use structural consistency at early samples as a confidence signal for adaptive compute allocation. For each instance: (1) sample N_min=4 extractions and compute structural agreement score S_4, (2) if S_4 >= theta_gate (high early agreement), accept the N=4 aggregation result and stop — the instance is 'easy' and further sampling is wasteful, (3) if S_4 < theta_gate, continue sampling to N_mid=8 and recompute S_8, (4) if S_8 >= theta_gate, accept the N=8 result, (5) otherwise, sample to N_max=16 or 32. We sweep theta_gate in {0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9} and report: average effective N per dataset (expected: 6-10x vs. fixed 32x), compute savings (target: 50-70% reduction with <0.5 F1 loss), and cost-accuracy Pareto frontiers comparing fixed-N vs. adaptive-N. This extends the adaptive TTS paradigm (DSC, Slim-SC, ReASC, CGES, Sonata) to structured prediction for the first time, where the key challenge is that the consistency signal itself requires structural alignment rather than simple answer agreement.
59	
60	*Learned Aggregation Scorer (LAS)*: Beyond hand-crafted threshold-based aggregation, we train a lightweight MLP (2 hidden layers, ~10K parameters) on Phase 0 pilot data to predict per-instance extraction quality from structural features. Input features (per-instance, computed from N samples): (i) span overlap distribution statistics (mean, variance, max of pairwise soft Jaccard across samples), (ii) type agreement entropy (entropy of predicted entity/relation type distributions across samples), (iii) consistency trajectory (agreement scores at N=4, 8, 16 — captures how consistency evolves with more samples), (iv) structural complexity features (number of predicted entities, relations, events per sample — captures extraction difficulty). The MLP outputs a scalar quality estimate used for: (a) sample selection (select the sample with highest predicted quality), (b) adaptive gating (use predicted quality as the confidence signal instead of raw structural agreement). We compare: hand-crafted aggregation vs. learned selection vs. learned gating, analyzing whether the learned scorer transfers across datasets (train on ACE05 pilot data, evaluate on SciERC/TACREV) and whether it improves over hand-crafted thresholds. The comparison between hand-crafted vs. learned aggregation is itself a finding — if learned aggregation helps significantly, it suggests structural consistency in IE is too complex for simple heuristics; if hand-crafted suffices, it validates the interpretability of our structural metrics.
61	
62	**Broader Applicability of ASCG to Structured Prediction**: While we demonstrate AS2CS through IE, the ASCG framework is the first general-purpose adaptive TTS method for any structured prediction task with non-scalar outputs. The core abstraction — sample multiple structured outputs, measure structural consistency via domain-appropriate alignment, and use consistency as a gating signal for adaptive compute allocation — transfers directly to: (1) semantic parsing, where SQL query graphs can be compared via AST edit distance and table/column overlap, and structural consistency identifies cases where the model is uncertain about join structure or predicate composition (cf. CSC-SQL's merge revision approach, which uses a task-specific correction model rather than general structural gating); (2) code generation, where AST-structured outputs enable tree-edit-distance-based consistency measurement beyond Functional Majority Voting's execution-dependent approach — particularly valuable for non-executable partial code or code in languages without test harnesses; (3) clinical NER and structured extraction, where FHIR-formatted outputs have hierarchical schema constraints and consistency across samples can identify uncertain entity boundaries and type assignments in medical text; (4) dialogue state tracking, where slot-value structures can be compared via slot-wise agreement and structural consistency identifies ambiguous user intents. In each case, the structural consistency metric and gating threshold require domain-specific instantiation, but the adaptive allocation framework (sample N_min, compute structural agreement, gate on consistency) is task-agnostic. We leave empirical validation on these domains to future work, focusing on IE as the most challenging case due to its multi-level compositional structure (entity → relation → event).
63	
64	**Ablation Framework**: Six baselines: (a) single-pass greedy (same model, no TTS), (b) random-of-N (lower bound), (c) naive majority voting (surface string matching, replicating PMC12888769), (d) oracle best-of-N (upper bound), (e) VerifiNER (KB-dependent paradigm comparison on NER subtasks), (f) fixed-N S2CS (uniform sampling without adaptive gating — to isolate ASCG contribution). The gap between oracle and single-pass bounds achievable gain; the gap between AS2CS and naive-majority isolates structural aggregation; the gap between fixed-N and adaptive-N isolates compute efficiency.
65	
66	**Error Taxonomy Analysis** (key analytical contribution): We categorize model errors into: (i) uncertainty errors — correct extraction appears in at least one of N samples but not deterministically (TTS can help), (ii) knowledge-gap errors — correct extraction never appears in any sample (TTS cannot help), (iii) systematic errors — model consistently produces the same wrong output (TTS cannot help). We report the fraction of each error type per dataset and subtask, directly addressing the knowledge-intensive limitation critique.
67	
68	**Headroom-Aware Analysis**: We correlate TTS gains with base single-pass performance level, testing the hypothesis that TTS is most effective for medium-difficulty subtasks (high enough base performance for meaningful samples, low enough ceiling for improvement room). This analysis helps practitioners predict where TTS is worth applying without running the full pipeline.
69	
70	**Compositional Consistency Analysis**: Following the 'Two Failures' work, we measure consistency at atomic (entity) vs. compositional (relation, event frame) granularity.
71	
72	**Evaluation**: 5 datasets — ACE05 (NER+RE+EE), Few-NERD (fine-grained NER, 66 entity types), SciERC (NER+RE), TACREV (sentence-level RE), WikiEvents (document-level EAE). We report F1 with bootstrap significance tests (p<0.05), scaling curves (F1 vs. N and vs. total compute), cost-accuracy Pareto frontiers for fixed-N vs. adaptive-N, error taxonomy distributions, and headroom gap correlations.

# Idea Brief: When Does Test-Time Scaling Help Structured Prediction? Adaptive Structural Self-Consistency with Learned Aggregation


- **Idea ID**: `idea_010`
- **Created**: 2026-05-14
- **Approved**: 2026-05-14
- **Source**: foreign:be-idea-gen-0509-6

## Seed Topic

Target: EMNLP 2026, ARR submission deadline 2026-05-25 (16 days from today 2026-05-09). Track: Information Extraction.

Direction: Structured information extraction — named entity recognition, relation extraction, event extraction, document-level IE, end-to-end extraction pipelines. Both LLM-based and non-LLM approaches welcome. In-scope: schema-guided extraction, zero-shot/few-shot IE, cross-document extraction, multimodal IE (text + layout + images), temporal/causal relation extraction.

Contribution type: METHOD ONLY. New extraction architectures, training strategies, or inference algorithms. Not a new dataset or annotation guideline.

HARD CONSTRAINTS:
1. Compute: ≤200 H100-hours total. IE work is typically lightweight — most experiments are fine-tuning or in-context learning.
2. Time: ≤16 days. Use existing IE frameworks (GoLLIE, UniNER, USM) or build on open LLMs with structured output.
3. Eval: ACE05, SciERC, TACRED/TACREV, DocRED, MAVEN, Few-NERD, WikiEvents, RAMS.

Look for: schema-guided extraction that generalizes across domains, efficient document-level IE beyond sliding windows, extraction with faithful provenance/citation, structured extraction from semi-structured sources (tables, forms, code). Avoid: basic NER fine-tuning, prompt-only extraction without architectural insight.

Tag: direction=information_extraction, contribution_type=method. target_venues=["EMNLP 2026 Main", "EMNLP 2026 Findings"].

## Core Problem

Test-time compute scaling (TTS) dramatically improves LLM reasoning on scalar-answer tasks, but structured prediction outputs — entity sets, relation graphs, event frames, SQL parse trees, dialogue states — have no clear verification function. Adaptive TTS methods (DSC, Slim-SC, ReASC, CGES, Sonata) further optimize compute allocation — but exclusively for scalar answers where consistency is trivially measured by answer agreement. We ask: when and why does sampling multiple schema-constrained structured outputs and aggregating via structural consistency improve prediction quality, how should compute be adaptively allocated across instances of varying structural complexity, and when does TTS fundamentally fail for structured prediction? We demonstrate through information extraction as the primary testbed, while establishing a general-purpose framework applicable to any structured prediction task.

## Opportunity / Why Now

TTS is the dominant paradigm for boosting LLM reasoning (DeepSeek-R1, o1), and a rapidly growing literature on adaptive TTS — DSC (NAACL 2025 Findings), Slim-SC (EMNLP 2025), ReASC (ACL 2026), CGES (arXiv 2511.02603), Sonata (ICLR 2026), CoRefine (arXiv 2602.08948), 'Learning When to Sample' (arXiv 2603.08999) — demonstrates that confidence-gated early stopping and difficulty-adaptive allocation can reduce sampling budgets by 45-80% with negligible accuracy loss. Yet this entire literature operates on scalar answers where consistency reduces to answer agreement. Two critical findings frame the gap for structured prediction: (1) PMC12888769 shows weak consistency-accuracy correlation for IE using surface-level Fleiss' Kappa on zero-shot models (Spearman 0.20-0.28), but the authors note that fine-tuned models 'could exhibit different consistency-accuracy dynamics'; (2) arXiv 2509.06861 argues TTS cannot help knowledge-intensive tasks because sampling cannot inject new information. We hypothesize that both findings admit an important exception: for fine-tuned models on structured prediction tasks, a significant fraction of errors are uncertainty-based (boundary detection, type ambiguity, structural composition) rather than knowledge-gap errors — and structural consistency (not surface string matching) can identify correct outputs in this regime. Moreover, structural consistency scores provide a natural gating signal for adaptive compute allocation: high early agreement signals easy instances where further sampling is wasteful, while low agreement signals hard instances requiring the full sampling budget. This opportunity extends beyond IE: any LLM task producing structured outputs — SQL queries, code ASTs, clinical FHIR resources, dialogue states — faces the same gap between scalar-answer TTS methods and structured prediction reality. XGrammar (MLSys 2025) makes constrained sampling near-free (<40 microseconds/token via vLLM's default backend), and mature UIE models (ProUIE, GoLLIE) provide strong base samplers. Concurrent work on multi-model NER ensembles (EL4NER, ACL 2025 submission) aggregates across different models, and CSC-SQL applies self-consistency to text-to-SQL via merge revision — but no work provides a general framework for adaptive structural self-consistency from a single fine-tuned model, isolating TTS contribution from model diversity and directly testing whether self-consistency scaling works for structured prediction.

## Landscape (SOTA & Limitations)

Test-time scaling is extensively studied for math/code (Forest-of-Thought, ICML 2025; Parallel TTS, Oct 2025; 30B+ token study, Dec 2024) but targets scalar-answer tasks exclusively. Self-consistency voting (Wang et al., ICLR 2023) and its successors — Reasoning-Aware Self-Consistency (NAACL 2025), inverse-entropy weighted voting (arXiv Nov 2025), Radial Consensus Score (arXiv April 2026), confidence-informed SC (arXiv Feb 2025), Ranked Voting SC (ACL 2025 Findings) — all aggregate scalar, embedding-space, or ranked-list answers. Critically, a mature and rapidly growing adaptive TTS literature optimizes compute allocation along a clear lineage: DSC (NAACL 2025 Findings) uses difficulty-based batch-level sample pre-allocation, ranking problems by difficulty and partitioning into easy/hard groups to adaptively allocate inference budgets; Slim-SC (EMNLP 2025) dynamically prunes redundant reasoning chains step-by-step during generation based on inter-chain semantic similarity, achieving up to 45% latency reduction; ReASC (ACL 2026) reframes adaptive sampling from response counting to evidence sufficiency via two-stage reliability-aware accumulation achieving 70% cost reduction; CGES (arXiv 2511.02603) forms Bayesian posteriors over candidate answers for principled early stopping with 69.4% call reduction; Sonata (ICLR 2026) trains a lightweight adapter to predict self-consistency from hidden states for thinking budget allocation (20-60% reduction); CoRefine (arXiv 2602.08948) uses a 211k-parameter Conv1D controller for HALT/RETHINK/ALTERNATIVE decisions with 63% wall-clock speedup; 'Learning When to Sample' (arXiv 2603.08999) achieves 80% token reduction via confidence-aware gating. The 'Reasoning on a Budget' survey (arXiv 2507.02076) provides a comprehensive taxonomy of adaptive TTC methods. However, all these methods define consistency and confidence over scalar answers — none addresses structured outputs where consistency measurement itself is non-trivial. In adjacent structured prediction domains, Functional Majority Voting (arXiv 2604.15618) aggregates code generation samples via execution-based functional equivalence — but this relies on executability, inapplicable to IE or most structured prediction tasks. CSC-SQL applies self-consistency with merge revision to text-to-SQL, but uses a task-specific correction model rather than a general structural consistency framework. STED (arXiv 2512.23712, NeurIPS 2025 Workshop) introduces Semantic Tree Edit Distance for measuring consistency of structured JSON outputs using Hungarian algorithm-based order-invariant matching and multi-level similarity, but functions as an evaluation framework rather than an improvement method — it measures consistency without leveraging it for aggregation or adaptive compute allocation. No work defines a general structural self-consistency framework for structured prediction outputs or uses it for adaptive compute gating. In IE specifically, ProUIE (April 2026) achieves SOTA via GRPO with stepwise fine-grained rewards on Qwen3-4B (ACE05-NER: 86.15 F1, ACE05-Arg: 52.58 F1, SciERC: 46.76 F1, avg NER: 79.44, avg RE: 71.17), and MR-UIE (Sept 2025) applies multi-perspective reasoning with RL — but both are training-time methods that generate single-pass outputs at inference. Post-hoc correction approaches include VerifiNER (ACL 2024) using KB-grounded verification and EL4NER (arXiv 2505.23038) ensembling multiple small LLMs for NER — but these are KB-dependent or multi-model approaches, fundamentally different from single-model self-consistency with adaptive gating. SaM (ACL 2025) dynamically selects and merges domain-specific NER expert models, again a multi-model approach. PMC12888769 (2026) measured consistency-accuracy correlation using Fleiss' Kappa on zero-shot hard-prompted models, finding weak Spearman correlations (0.20-0.28) — but used surface string matching on un-fine-tuned models while we propose structural consistency on task-specific fine-tuned models, and they acknowledged this limitation. The 'Two Failures of Self-Consistency' (Chen et al., 2023) demonstrates poor compositional consistency — IE has compositional structure (entity to relation to event) that may exhibit similar failures, which we explicitly test. No concurrent work applies adaptive test-time sampling with structural aggregation from a single fine-tuned model to any structured prediction task — confirmed via arXiv and OpenReview searches through May 2026.

## Proposed Approach

We propose Adaptive Structural Self-Consistency Scaling (AS2CS) as both a method and an empirical framework for understanding when adaptive TTS helps structured prediction, demonstrated through information extraction as a comprehensive testbed. The research is structured in three phases: pilot validation (Phase 0), full experimental study (Phase 1), and adaptive gating evaluation (Phase 2).

**Phase 0: Pilot Validation and Headroom Analysis (~8h H100, Days 1-3)**
Before committing to the full study, we run a targeted pilot to validate two premises. First, using 200 instances each from ACE05 NER and ACE05 EAE (event argument extraction), we sample N=8 extractions at T=1.0 from fine-tuned Qwen3-8B and compute: (a) Fleiss' Kappa on surface string matches (replicating PMC12888769), (b) our soft Jaccard span-level structural consistency score, and (c) Spearman correlation of each metric with per-instance F1 against gold annotations. If structural consistency yields significantly stronger correlation than Fleiss' Kappa (target: Spearman >=0.40 vs. their 0.20-0.28), we proceed. Second, we compute oracle best-of-N F1 gaps per dataset and subtask at N=8 to establish headroom ceilings: if oracle best-of-8 exceeds single-pass by <1 F1 on a subtask, TTS gains are fundamentally ceiling-limited there. We use headroom gaps to prioritize analysis: high-headroom subtasks (likely EAE at ~52 F1, SciERC RE at ~47 F1) receive full experimental treatment, while low-headroom subtasks (likely ACE05 NER near ~87 F1) are analyzed primarily for negative/diagnostic insight. Phase 0 also generates training data for the learned aggregation scorer (Phase 2). If both metrics show weak correlation (<=0.30) even with structural consistency, we pivot to a negative/analytical result.

**Base Models**: Qwen3-8B fine-tuned on UIE instruction data (JSON output format, trained with LLaMA Factory following ProUIE's pipeline) as primary model, and GoLLIE-7B as a cross-architecture generalization check.

**Sampling**: For each input, we sample N in {4, 8, 16, 32} schema-constrained extractions via XGrammar-backed structured generation in vLLM with temperature T=1.0 (standard for self-consistency sampling, maximizing output diversity), enforcing valid JSON output at near-zero overhead.

**Phase 1: Structural Consistency Aggregation (Full Study)**
Three aggregation functions tailored to IE subtask structure: (1) span-level entity voting via soft Jaccard similarity over character offsets with type-aware grouping (threshold tau_span), (2) relation-level graph consensus via edge majority voting after entity coreference alignment using mention overlap (threshold tau_coref), (3) event-level frame aggregation via trigger-anchored slot matching with role-wise majority voting (threshold tau_trigger). A composite structural agreement score ranks candidates or constructs a merged consensus output.

**Aggregation Hyperparameter Sensitivity Analysis**: Each aggregation function depends on a threshold parameter. We report sensitivity sweeps: tau_span in {0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.8}, tau_coref in {0.3, 0.5, 0.7}, tau_trigger in {0.5, 0.7, 0.9}. We report F1 variance across threshold settings per dataset.

**Phase 2: Adaptive Gating and Learned Aggregation**

*Adaptive Structural Consistency Gating (ASCG)*: Rather than applying a fixed N=32 samples uniformly, we use structural consistency at early samples as a confidence signal for adaptive compute allocation. For each instance: (1) sample N_min=4 extractions and compute structural agreement score S_4, (2) if S_4 >= theta_gate (high early agreement), accept the N=4 aggregation result and stop — the instance is 'easy' and further sampling is wasteful, (3) if S_4 < theta_gate, continue sampling to N_mid=8 and recompute S_8, (4) if S_8 >= theta_gate, accept the N=8 result, (5) otherwise, sample to N_max=16 or 32. We sweep theta_gate in {0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9} and report: average effective N per dataset (expected: 6-10x vs. fixed 32x), compute savings (target: 50-70% reduction with <0.5 F1 loss), and cost-accuracy Pareto frontiers comparing fixed-N vs. adaptive-N. This extends the adaptive TTS paradigm (DSC, Slim-SC, ReASC, CGES, Sonata) to structured prediction for the first time, where the key challenge is that the consistency signal itself requires structural alignment rather than simple answer agreement.

*Learned Aggregation Scorer (LAS)*: Beyond hand-crafted threshold-based aggregation, we train a lightweight MLP (2 hidden layers, ~10K parameters) on Phase 0 pilot data to predict per-instance extraction quality from structural features. Input features (per-instance, computed from N samples): (i) span overlap distribution statistics (mean, variance, max of pairwise soft Jaccard across samples), (ii) type agreement entropy (entropy of predicted entity/relation type distributions across samples), (iii) consistency trajectory (agreement scores at N=4, 8, 16 — captures how consistency evolves with more samples), (iv) structural complexity features (number of predicted entities, relations, events per sample — captures extraction difficulty). The MLP outputs a scalar quality estimate used for: (a) sample selection (select the sample with highest predicted quality), (b) adaptive gating (use predicted quality as the confidence signal instead of raw structural agreement). We compare: hand-crafted aggregation vs. learned selection vs. learned gating, analyzing whether the learned scorer transfers across datasets (train on ACE05 pilot data, evaluate on SciERC/TACREV) and whether it improves over hand-crafted thresholds. The comparison between hand-crafted vs. learned aggregation is itself a finding — if learned aggregation helps significantly, it suggests structural consistency in IE is too complex for simple heuristics; if hand-crafted suffices, it validates the interpretability of our structural metrics.

**Broader Applicability of ASCG to Structured Prediction**: While we demonstrate AS2CS through IE, the ASCG framework is the first general-purpose adaptive TTS method for any structured prediction task with non-scalar outputs. The core abstraction — sample multiple structured outputs, measure structural consistency via domain-appropriate alignment, and use consistency as a gating signal for adaptive compute allocation — transfers directly to: (1) semantic parsing, where SQL query graphs can be compared via AST edit distance and table/column overlap, and structural consistency identifies cases where the model is uncertain about join structure or predicate composition (cf. CSC-SQL's merge revision approach, which uses a task-specific correction model rather than general structural gating); (2) code generation, where AST-structured outputs enable tree-edit-distance-based consistency measurement beyond Functional Majority Voting's execution-dependent approach — particularly valuable for non-executable partial code or code in languages without test harnesses; (3) clinical NER and structured extraction, where FHIR-formatted outputs have hierarchical schema constraints and consistency across samples can identify uncertain entity boundaries and type assignments in medical text; (4) dialogue state tracking, where slot-value structures can be compared via slot-wise agreement and structural consistency identifies ambiguous user intents. In each case, the structural consistency metric and gating threshold require domain-specific instantiation, but the adaptive allocation framework (sample N_min, compute structural agreement, gate on consistency) is task-agnostic. We leave empirical validation on these domains to future work, focusing on IE as the most challenging case due to its multi-level compositional structure (entity → relation → event).

**Ablation Framework**: Six baselines: (a) single-pass greedy (same model, no TTS), (b) random-of-N (lower bound), (c) naive majority voting (surface string matching, replicating PMC12888769), (d) oracle best-of-N (upper bound), (e) VerifiNER (KB-dependent paradigm comparison on NER subtasks), (f) fixed-N S2CS (uniform sampling without adaptive gating — to isolate ASCG contribution). The gap between oracle and single-pass bounds achievable gain; the gap between AS2CS and naive-majority isolates structural aggregation; the gap between fixed-N and adaptive-N isolates compute efficiency.

**Error Taxonomy Analysis** (key analytical contribution): We categorize model errors into: (i) uncertainty errors — correct extraction appears in at least one of N samples but not deterministically (TTS can help), (ii) knowledge-gap errors — correct extraction never appears in any sample (TTS cannot help), (iii) systematic errors — model consistently produces the same wrong output (TTS cannot help). We report the fraction of each error type per dataset and subtask, directly addressing the knowledge-intensive limitation critique.

**Headroom-Aware Analysis**: We correlate TTS gains with base single-pass performance level, testing the hypothesis that TTS is most effective for medium-difficulty subtasks (high enough base performance for meaningful samples, low enough ceiling for improvement room). This analysis helps practitioners predict where TTS is worth applying without running the full pipeline.

**Compositional Consistency Analysis**: Following the 'Two Failures' work, we measure consistency at atomic (entity) vs. compositional (relation, event frame) granularity.

**Evaluation**: 5 datasets — ACE05 (NER+RE+EE), Few-NERD (fine-grained NER, 66 entity types), SciERC (NER+RE), TACREV (sentence-level RE), WikiEvents (document-level EAE). We report F1 with bootstrap significance tests (p<0.05), scaling curves (F1 vs. N and vs. total compute), cost-accuracy Pareto frontiers for fixed-N vs. adaptive-N, error taxonomy distributions, and headroom gap correlations.

[Related Work / 新增三个方向] — **从仅覆盖 adaptive self-consistency 扩展到六个方向**：原始 proposal 仅引用 DSC/Slim-SC/ReASC/CGES/Sonata/STED。修改为增加：(a) classical structured prediction ensemble methods, (b) LLM confidence estimation for structured outputs, (c) test-time augmentation for NLP, (d) TTS for non-scalar generative NLP + code generation structural consistency (CodeT, MBR-based selection), (e) LLM calibration for structured tasks。每个方向明确差异化定位。加深 STED 讨论：STED = evaluation, AS2CS = aggregation + adaptive gating + diagnostic framework。 — 命中 Related Work

17. [统计方案 / Evaluation Metrics] — **增加显著性检验和多 seed 报告**：原始 proposal 未指定统计检验。修改为 paired bootstrap test (n=10000) + 95% CI，3-5 random seeds 的 mean±std，significance threshold "≥ 2 F1 with p < 0.05"。 — 命中 Technical Soundness

18. [Significance 底线 / Motivation] — **显式声明何种增益算 meaningful**：原始 proposal 无此声明。修改为 "≥ 2 F1 points or ≥ 30% cost reduction at equivalent F1"，展示作者的 self-awareness。 — 命中 Soundness + 评审印象

19. [Paper Organization / 新增段落] — **增加 main vs. appendix 分配策略**：原始 proposal 无此规划，所有实验并列。修改为：正文聚焦 pilot validation 核心结果 + ASCG vs. baselines 主表 + diagnostic heatmap (signature figure) + error taxonomy 分布；所有 ablation 放 appendix；RQ3/RQ4 正文各 1-2 段。缓解 "tries to do too much" 的常见 reviewer 批评。 — 命中 Technical Soundness + Presentation

20. [Cost Framing / Introduction + Experiments] — **增加 concrete cost-efficiency metrics**：原始 proposal 用抽象的 "compute-efficient" 表述。修改为报告具体的 average samples saved、cost-accuracy Pareto 改进百分比，总 cost 定义包含 LLM sampling + alignment overhead + gating overhead（honest accounting），并报告 wall-clock time breakdown per complexity bin。 — 命中 Significance + Practical Impact

【主要风险】:

1. **Algorithmic novelty 的结构性 ceiling**：即使叙事重构为"诊断范式"，ASCG/LAS 的核心技术组件（已有对齐算法 + 标准 MLP + 常规 gating loop）仍然缺乏 algorithmic novelty。如果 1-2 位 reviewer 坚持要 novel algorithm 而非 novel analysis/diagnostic，论文可能被定性为 "systematic empirical study" 并被降分。这是结构性限制，无法通过 proposal 优化进一步缓解——只能靠实验结果的 surprising 程度（特别是 phase transition 发现或 dramatic fine-tuning effect）来补偿。

2. **Pilot validation 失败的 pivot 风险**：如果 fine-tuned 模型的 ρ < 0.4 across the board（即结构化 consistency 即使用 alignment-based metrics 也无法作为可靠 confidence proxy），论文必须 pivot 为 negative finding。虽然 dual-outcome 设计使这在学术上是可发表的，但 negative finding 论文的 EMNLP 主会接受概率显著低于 positive finding（估计降至 20-25%），且论文的 primary contribution（diagnostic framework）将失去其 prescriptive value（只剩 descriptive value）。

【实施评估】:

- **计算资源**: 需要至少 1 × A100-80GB（或等价）用于 Qwen3-8B/GoLLIE-7B 的 fine-tuning 和多次采样推理；Qwen3-32B fine-tuning + 推理需要 2-4 × A100-80GB 或 1 × H100。5 个 benchmark × 4 模型配置 × N=8-16 采样 × 多 seed = 大量推理，预估总 GPU 时长 200-400 A100-hours（含 fine-tuning ~50h + 推理 ~150-350h）。如用云平台（AWS/GCP），约 $600-$1200。LLM-as-judge baseline (baseline 7) 如果用 API model 会有额外 API 成本，约 $100-$300。
- **数据需求**: ACE05、Few-NERD、SciERC、TACREV、WikiEvents 五个 benchmark 均公开可得。ACE05 需要 LDC 许可证（大多数学术机构已有）。UIE 格式的 fine-tuning 数据需要从原始数据集转换，转换脚本已有公开实现。无需构建新数据集。
- **人工介入**: 不需要人工标注（所有 benchmark 自带 gold annotation）。Error taxonomy 分类完全自动化（基于 gold 对比的操作性定义）。需要研究者人工检查 ~50-100 个 error classification 实例做 sanity check（约 2-4 小时）。LAS feature importance 的 SHAP 分析结果需要研究者解读。整体人工介入量低。
- **训练需求**: 需要模型训练。(a) Qwen3-8B fine-tuning on UIE tasks（~10-15h on 1×A100）；(b) Qwen3-32B fine-tuning（~20-30h on 2-4×A100）；(c) GoLLIE-7B 可能需要适配训练或直接用预训练版本；(d) LAS MLP 训练极轻（CPU 级别，分钟级）。总训练时长约 30-50 GPU-hours。
- **新 Benchmark**: 不需要构建新 benchmark。所有评测在已有公开 benchmark 上进行。但需要构建 complexity-binned evaluation splits（按 entity count、relation depth 等分层），这是对现有数据的重新组织而非新建。
- **预估周期**: 从启动到可投稿约 **8-10 周**。细分：Week 1-2 数据准备 + fine-tuning；Week 2-3 Pilot validation（决定 proceed/pivot）；Week 3-6 主实验（ASCG vs. baselines × 5 benchmarks × 多配置）；Week 5-7 ablation studies + diagnostic heatmap 构建；Week 7-9 写作；Week 9-10 内部 rev


## MVP Validation Results

- **Date**: 2026-05-14
- **Hypothesis Supported**: Yes

### Key Metrics

NER full rho_sj=0.388 (SJ>FK +6.6pp, p=2e-20) | RE full rho_sj=0.234 (FAIL <0.30) | RE cond rho_sj=0.372 (SJ>FK +11.8pp) | RE pct_zero=42.4% | NER oracle headroom=+5.5pp | RE oracle headroom=+13.1pp | Gate 0: NER F1=66.2%, RE F1=42.1%

### Summary

MVP 验证 structural self-consistency 作为 IE test-time scaling 信号。5 轮 pilot 实验（ft_001/ft_002_v2 模型，T=1.0/0.7，N=8，SciERC 551 instances）+ 1 轮度量分解诊断。结果：NER 方向强正向（rho_sj=0.388, SJ>FK p=2e-20）；RE full-set FAIL（rho_sj=0.234<0.30），但 RE conditional set（排除 all-zero knowledge-gap 实例）显示强信号（rho_sj=0.372, SJ>FK 11.8pp）。E1 诊断排除了度量设计问题——RE weakness 是复合错误传播的固有属性。T=0.7 vs T=1.0 对比揭示采样温度对信号质量的影响。假设部分验证：entity-level IE 有效，relation-level 需 capability-aware 分析。

### Recommendation

GO — 进入 research 阶段，走 Narrative A（NER-primary + RE diagnostic）。NER 信号足够强且 SJ>FK 优势一致。RE conditional 分析 + E1 诊断 + 温度敏感性分析为论文增加诊断深度。下一步：E3 (NER N=16 验证 rho 是否过 0.40) + E4 (NER 多数据集泛化 CoNLL/OntoNotes) + RE 诊断整理。目标 ARR May 2026-05-25。

# When Self-Consistency Fails for NER: Degeneracy, Signal Collapse, and the Correlation-Selection Gap

Code for the paper "When Self-Consistency Fails for NER: Degeneracy, Signal Collapse, and the Correlation-Selection Gap" (anonymous submission).

## Overview

This repository provides the implementation for studying test-time compute scaling (self-consistency and best-of-N) for Named Entity Recognition. We characterize when scaling succeeds and fails using NER as the primary testbed (SciERC, CoNLL-2003, Few-NERD, WNUT-17), with cross-task pilots on relation extraction and SQL parsing.

Key components:
- **Sampling**: Multi-sample inference with vLLM + XGrammar constrained decoding (`code/sampling.py`)
- **Consistency metrics**: Fleiss' Kappa, structural soft Jaccard, log-probability signals (`code/consistency.py`, `code/unified_metrics.py`)
- **Evaluation**: Strict-match NER F1, per-instance correlation analysis (`code/evaluation.py`)
- **Selection & Construction**: Entity-level consensus construction, MBR selection, adaptive budget allocation (`code/entity_construction*.py`, `code/ccs_selection.py`)
- **Diagnostic framework**: Degeneracy detection, signal collapse analysis, correlation-selection gap diagnostics (`code/analysis_dgs_*.py`)

## Requirements

- Python 3.10+
- PyTorch 2.1+
- vLLM (for multi-sample inference with constrained decoding)
- Transformers, Datasets
- LLaMA-Factory (for LoRA fine-tuning)
- NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, matplotlib

Install dependencies:
```bash
pip install torch vllm transformers datasets accelerate scipy scikit-learn matplotlib seaborn tqdm
```

## Data Preparation

### Datasets
- **SciERC**: `code/data_utils.py` handles loading and conversion
- **CoNLL-2003**: `code/convert_conll2003.py`
- **Few-NERD**: `code/convert_fewnerd.py`
- **WNUT-17**: `code/convert_wnut17.py`

Convert datasets to the unified UIE JSON format:
```bash
python code/convert_conll2003.py
python code/convert_fewnerd.py
python code/convert_wnut17.py
```

The conversion scripts download datasets from HuggingFace and produce LLaMA-Factory compatible JSON files in `data/`.

### Models

We use LoRA fine-tuned models:
- **Qwen3-8B** (primary): fine-tuned with configs in `configs/train/`
- **Qwen3-4B**: scale ablation
- **LLaMA-3.1-8B / LLaMA-3.2-3B**: cross-architecture check
- **Qwen2.5-32B**: larger-scale experiment

Fine-tune with LLaMA-Factory:
```bash
llamafactory-cli train configs/train/train_config_scierc_3ep.yaml
```

Export (merge LoRA weights):
```bash
llamafactory-cli export configs/export/export_config_scierc_3epoch.yaml
```

## Running Experiments

### 1. Multi-Sample Inference

The sampling pipeline generates N constrained samples per instance:
```bash
python code/sampling.py \
    --model_path ./models/merged_model \
    --dataset scierc \
    --n_samples 16 \
    --temperature 1.0
```

### 2. Signal Analysis (5-Signal Pipeline)

Compute all quality estimation signals (MV, SJ, LP, VC, EM) for sampled outputs:
```bash
python code/eval_n16_5signal.py        # SciERC N=16
python code/exp021_fewnerd_full_analysis.py  # Few-NERD
python code/analyze_exp002_conll2003.py      # CoNLL-2003
python code/wnut17_full_signal_analysis.py   # WNUT-17
```

### 3. Selection & Construction

Entity-level consensus construction and sample selection:
```bash
python code/entity_construction_fair.py  # Fair entity construction
python code/ccs_selection.py            # Cascaded consistency selection
python code/compute_selection_f1.py     # Selection F1 evaluation
```

### 4. Diagnostic Analysis

Degeneracy-gated selection and signal collapse analysis:
```bash
python code/analysis_dgs_full_validation.py  # Full DGS validation
python code/analysis_dgs_multiseed.py        # Multi-seed DGS analysis
python code/analysis_dgs_cross_model.py      # Cross-model analysis
```

### 5. Adaptive Budget

Adaptive compute allocation experiments:
```bash
python b7_adaptive_budget.py
python b7_adaptive_budget_v2.py
```

### 6. Bootstrap Significance Tests

```bash
python run_bootstrap_loo.py       # Leave-one-out bootstrap
python bootstrap_analysis.py      # Bootstrap significance analysis
```

## Project Structure

```
.
├── code/                    # Core modules and analysis scripts
│   ├── sampling.py          # vLLM multi-sample inference
│   ├── consistency.py       # Consistency metrics (FK, SJ, LP)
│   ├── evaluation.py        # NER/RE evaluation
│   ├── unified_metrics.py   # Unified F1 and degeneracy detection
│   ├── data_utils.py        # Data loading and conversion
│   ├── entity_construction*.py  # Entity consensus construction
│   ├── analysis_dgs_*.py    # Degeneracy-gated selection analysis
│   ├── probe/               # Hidden-state probing experiments
│   └── pipeline/            # Multi-stage pipeline scripts
├── scripts/                 # Experiment post-processing and analysis
├── configs/                 # Training and export configurations
│   ├── train/               # LLaMA-Factory training configs
│   ├── export/              # LoRA merge/export configs
│   └── lora/                # LoRA adapter configs
├── experiments/             # Cross-task pilot experiments
│   ├── fewrel_re_sc/        # Relation extraction pilot
│   └── humaneval_sc/        # Code generation pilot
├── examples/
│   └── deepspeed/           # DeepSpeed ZeRO-2 config
└── *.py, *.sh               # Top-level experiment scripts
```

## Reproducing Key Results

### Table 2: Selection F1 (5-Signal Comparison)
```bash
python code/table2_selection_f1.py
```

### Correlation-Selection Gap Analysis
```bash
python code/exp010_selection_curves.py
```

### Degeneracy Analysis
```bash
python code/analysis_degen_gated_selection.py
python code/batch_recalc_degeneracy.py
```

### Temperature Ablation
```bash
python code/adaptive_temperature_analysis.py
python code/analyze_exp026_temp_5signal.py
```

### N-Scaling Curves
```bash
python code/lp_best_n_scaling.py
python scripts/n_scaling_gf_maxlp.py
```

This code is released for research purposes under the MIT License.
